transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-23
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 1:12:00 (approx)
Attendees: Jesse (Redwood AE), Nina (Redwood SE), Marta (Lighthouse), Ravi (Lighthouse SRE), Elena (Product), Tom (Security), Asha (Data Eng)

Summary:
Quick kickoff to align on pilot success criteria for inference serving. Main focus: define which latency SLOs we'll measure (TTFT vs TPOT), decide p95/p99 targets, agree sampling methodology, and set bench/traffic handoff timeline. Also touched on security (KMS, VPC), and contract/pricing bands for Dedicated vs Hosted.

Topics:
- TTFT (time-to-first-token) vs TPOT (total per-token) tradeoffs
- p95/p99 target setting and tail behavior
- Workload sizing: qps, payload distribution, token lengths
- Benchmark plan: baseline, noise, warm cache vs cold, KV/prefix caching
- Timeline and deliverables for a 4-week pilot

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jesse (Redwood AE): okay, uh, thanks everyone for joining, we're, we're on the call to get aligned on the lighthouse pilot, specifically the latency SLOs and the measurement plan. um Nina from our SE team will lead the bench details.
[00:18] Marta (Lighthouse): thanks Jesse, appreciate it. quick context — we have an internal voice of clinician product, so latency is, is pretty sensitive for user flows. we call out both first-token experience and total response time in the product goals.
[00:34] Nina (Redwood SE): great, can you give a quick sketch of traffic? like typical qps, tokens per request, streaming vs non-stream?
[00:41] Ravi (SRE): yeah so right now average qps is about 12 during peak for the pilot cohort, payload sizes vary — median 48 tokens, mean closer to 80, we do a small amount of streaming, maybe 8% of calls.
[00:56] Elena (Product): we have two critical paths — short clinical prompts (quick lookups) and longer conversational triage flows. short ones need sub-300ms TTFT ideally.
[01:12] Tom (Security): just a heads up we'll need KMS integration and audit logs for any pilot environment that touches PHI-ish data, even if anonymized. SOC 2 checklist applies.
[01:26] Jesse (Redwood AE): got it. Nina, on TTFT vs TPOT, what's the recommended approach for this workload?
[01:34] Nina (Redwood SE): in practice you want both metrics. TTFT matters for perceived interactivity, TPOT captures full latency cost and tail. For pilot we usually measure p50/p95/p99 for both, plus a per-request token breakdown. Two gotchas: caching can make TPOT look better after warmup, and batching helps TPOT but can hurt TTFT.
[02:01] Marta: can you explain caching gotcha?
[02:04] Nina: sure — prefix/KV caching reduces repeated attention compute, so many subsequent requests show much lower TPOT. for a realistic pilot we need a cold-start measurement and an operational warm profile.
[02:18] Ravi: how do you recommend sampling? we don't want to send full production traffic but want representative tail.
[02:25] Nina: provide a 48–72 hour capture of requests with tokens and timestamps; we'll bootstrap a traffic generator that replays at scaled qps. important to preserve inter-arrival and token distribution, and mark streaming calls. We'll run a sweep of 3 load points: baseline (0.5x current peak), peak (1x), and burst (2x) to observe degradation modes.
[02:51] Marta: ok that sounds reasonable. p95/p99 targets — what should we aim for?
[02:56] Jesse: show some typical numbers — Nina?
[02:59] Nina: for models in our catalog, short prompts (<=64 tokens) we target TTFT p95 < 250ms, p99 < 450ms; TPOT p95 < 420ms, p99 < 900ms as rough starting points. for longer prompts (256–512 tokens) TTFT is similar but TPOT obviously increases; it's more important to define acceptance bands per payload bucket.
[03:26] Ravi: those p99 numbers seem optimistic if we're on shared hosted. if we go Dedicated does that substantially tighten the tail?
[03:33] Nina: yes Dedicated gives you more predictable hardware and isolation so tails are tighter. we can model expected variance from our historical runs and produce a per-setup SLO projection.
[03:45] Tom: security question — if we're going Dedicated on your infra vs private VPC deployment, what's the difference for KMS and audit logs?
[03:54] Jesse: Dedicated can still integrate with your KMS via customer-managed keys; Private/VPC gives you full control and on-prem options but involves longer lead times and separate contract. we'll include a matrix in the pilot charter.
[04:07] Elena: timeline? we said 4 weeks pilot, what's realistic for handoff and benchmark runs?
[04:12] Nina: week 0 — traffic capture + contract + infra prep; week 1 — baseline runs (cold/warm) at low load; week 2 — scale runs at peak and burst; week 3 — tuning and retest; week 4 — analysis, report, and go/no-go. so about 4 weeks in total assuming infra access and sample corpus within 3 business days.
[04:36] Marta: fine, but what's the success criteria?
[04:39] Jesse: success is multi-part: meet TTFT and TPOT targets for 90% of sampled traffic per bucket, no functional regression in output quality, and acceptable cost per effective request within agreed bound. we'll spell exact thresholds in the charter.
[04:56] Ravi: what sample sizes do you need to validate p99 reliably?
[04:59] Nina: p99 is noisy — we want at least 10k samples per payload bucket to have confidence. if that's not possible we'll run longer duration or synthetic amplification while being careful with caching artifacts.
[05:15] Asha (Data Eng): we can share 7 days of anonymized logs and a 5k sample corpus tomorrow.
[05:20] Nina: that helps. also worth instrumenting to capture CPU/GPU util and queueing to correlate with tail.
[05:27] Marta: can you show example plots we should expect in the deliverable?
[05:31] Nina: yes — p50/p95/p99 latency curves by token bucket, concurrency vs tail, CPU/GPU utilization timelines, and a heatmap of request qps vs latency. we'll include a CSV and a short slide deck.
[05:45] Jesse: on pricing and pilot scope — we propose two bands: Hosted API pilot for quick start, and Dedicated pilot when you want committed capacity. pricing will be usage + a short-term reserved capacity estimate for Dedicated. I'll attach the numbers after the call.
[05:58] Ravi: how do you control batching in hosted environment? we don't want long queuing to improve TPOT at expense of TTFT.
[06:05] Nina: we expose batching and latency SLO knobs; for pilot we'll set batching thresholds to prioritize TTFT for short prompts, and test relaxed batching for TPOT efficiency. we'll report effective queuing time.
[06:18] Tom: audit trail — we need request-level logging with anonymized IDs and timestamp correlation to our SIEM. is that available?
[06:25] Jesse: yes, audit logs and trace export are supported; we'll scope retention and export methods in the contract appendix.
[06:33] Marta: any competitive ops we should be aware of? we've talked to Vertex and a smaller infra vendor, mainly about pricing.
[06:40] Jesse: competition noted. our angle is production predictability and rollouts — canary, fallback to smaller model variants during congestion.
[06:49] Elena: fallback policy — important. if we miss p99 by a lot during burst what do we do?
[06:54] Nina: we define automatic fallback chains: same model lower precision/quantized variant, then a smaller model; we measure quality deltas and have a threshold for auto-fallback. part of the pilot will measure quality loss vs latency gains.
[07:10] Ravi: last thing — do you provide scripts to replay traffic exactly for the bench? we prefer repeatability.
[07:14] Nina: yes, we feed the replay harness with captured traffic CSV, can do deterministic seeds, and include options to simulate client-side think time. we'll share the harness repo link.
[07:24] Marta: let's recap next steps quickly.
[07:27] Jesse: recap: Lighthouse will share logs and sample corpus by 8/25; Nina will run initial bench and share results by 8/27; Jesse will send pilot charter and pricing by 8/28; Security (Tom) will confirm KMS and SOC2 items by 8/26.
[07:43] Tom: sounds good.
[07:45] Jesse: thanks all. we'll follow up with calendar invites for the bench kickoff.
[07:50] (call ends)
